title: Hyderabad-Born Dipika Damerla Woos Voters With Bollywood-Style Mississauga Mayoral Pitch
excerpt: The Hyderabad-born Ward 7 councillor and former Ontario cabinet minister is polling at 10–13% in the October 26 mayoral race against Carolyn Parrish, Bonnie Crombie and Alvin Tedjo.
body:
• Hyderabad-born Dipika Damerla, a two-term Mississauga councillor and former Ontario cabinet minister, is running for mayor of Mississauga in the October 26 municipal election — and has gone to voters with a Bollywood-style video appeal, NDTV reported.
  • She is one of four leading contenders, alongside incumbent Carolyn Parrish, former mayor Bonnie Crombie and councillor Alvin Tedjo. Polls put her at 10–13%, with roughly a third of voters still undecided.
  • Her platform: a freeze on property taxes, an independent Auditor General for the city, and fixing a police-funding formula under which Mississauga carries 62% of the Peel police budget against Brampton's 38%.
  • Advance voting ran October 6–11; election day is Monday, October 26. One in four Mississauga residents is South Asian, and the city has never elected an ethnic mayor.

The Mississauga mayor's race has picked up a Bollywood beat. Hyderabad-born city councillor Dipika Damerla, one of four leading candidates in the October 26 municipal election, has released a Bollywood-style video appeal to voters, according to NDTV — the first time a candidate in the race has drawn so directly on Indian popular culture to make a campaign pitch.

The appeal is aimed squarely at the constituency where Damerla's political identity runs deepest. Mississauga is changing: 62% of its residents identify as a visible minority and one in four identifies as South Asian, yet the city has never elected an ethnic mayor. In a contest dominated by the bruising Parrish–Crombie rematch, Damerla's Bollywood turn is both a campaign tactic and a statement about who the city's voters are.

Context & Background

Damerla's resume is among the deepest of any candidate in the field. Born in Hyderabad, Telangana, and educated at the University of Toronto, she served as the Liberal MPP for Mississauga East—Cooksville from 2011 to 2018, holding cabinet posts as Associate Minister for Long-Term Care and Wellness and then as Minister of Seniors Affairs under Premier Kathleen Wynne.

https://x.com/smitaprakash/status/2108737897205825986

She has represented Ward 7 (Cooksville) on Mississauga city council since December 2018. This is her second run at the mayor's chair: she placed third with 19.4% in the 2024 byelection that followed Bonnie Crombie's departure to lead the Ontario Liberal Party, a race won by Carolyn Parrish.

The 2026 rematch has drawn 14 candidates, but polling has consistently shown a four-person race. A Pallas Data survey on September 14 put Parrish at 32%, Crombie at 27%, Tedjo at 19% and Damerla at 12%, with a third of voters undecided. A Mainstreet snapshot in early October had Crombie at 30.4% and Parrish at 27.6%, with Tedjo at 20.5% and Damerla at 10.4%. Liaison Strategies' August survey showed Parrish and Crombie tied at 26%, Damerla at 13% and Tedjo at 9%.

Impact & Analysis

Damerla's platform is built on affordability and accountability. In her campaign launch she promised a property-tax freeze, an independent Auditor General, and value-for-money audits of policing — arguing that Mississauga carries 62% of the Peel police budget compared with 38% for Brampton, on a formula she says is decades out of date.

"My ambition for Mississauga is not to be a big city. Oh no. My ambition for Mississauga is to be a great city."

— Dipika Damerla, at her campaign launch

Her challenge is visibility. Two televised debates — the Board of Trade debate at Sheridan College in late September and a CityNews debate on October 1 — were dominated by personal exchanges between Parrish and Crombie. A Liaison poll taken October 2–4 found 74% of residents say personal insults are unacceptable in the campaign, and only 14% describe the campaign as mostly respectful. In a race where voters say they want substance, a candidate running on audits and funding formulas may yet find an opening — the Bollywood appeal is Damerla's attempt to break through the noise on her own terms.

Diaspora Angle

For the Indian diaspora, Damerla's candidacy is the most prominent South Asian bid for a major Canadian city's top job in recent memory. Mississauga's South Asian community — roughly 190,000 people — has long been an electoral force at the provincial and federal level; the mayor's office is the one door that has never opened. Whether her Bollywood-style outreach moves votes or simply adds colour to the campaign, it signals a candidate comfortable speaking to her community in its own cultural language rather than through the usual translations of Canadian campaigning.

What's Next

Advance voting closed October 11, and the race now enters its final two weeks. The open question is turnout: only 21.84% of eligible voters cast ballots in the 2022 municipal election, rising to 25.7% in the 2024 byelection. Political scientist Randy Besco of the University of Toronto Mississauga notes that competitive races tend to draw more voters — and with a third of the electorate undecided, the outcome is far from settled. Election day is Monday, October 26.
